title: Beam Reactions and Equilibrium Explorer
description: Students will calculate (Bloom Level 3, Apply) the support reactions of a simply supported beam by applying the three equilibrium conditions, and will analyze (Bloom Level 4, Analyze) how moving a load changes the share carried by each support.
creator: The Science of the Built Environment
author: Dan McCreary
subject: The Science of the Built Environment
chapter_title: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings

pedagogical.learningObjective: Calculate the support reactions of a simply supported beam by applying the three equilibrium conditions, and analyze how moving a load changes the share carried by each support.
recommendedUsage: Set the beam span and the load with the sliders. Drag the orange load arrow along the beam, or use the Dist. from A slider. The reaction arrows at A and B resize as you move it.

Read the equation panel: it substitutes the current numbers into the moment, vertical-force, and horizontal-force equations and shows an equilibrium check. Hover over any arrow to see its name and value.
Press Step through to reveal the three equations one at a time, in the order you would solve them by hand: moments about A, then vertical forces, then horizontal forces.
Switch to Uniform (plf) to see a line load act as one force at midspan, then check Remove support B to see the beam rotate about A because the moment equation can no longer be satisfied.
activities: Warm-up (5 min): Students predict RA and RB for the Riverbend beam (6,000 lb, 10 ft from A on a 40 ft span), then check against the sim.
Explore (10 min): Students move the load to five positions and record RA and RB, then describe in words how the share changes as the load nears a support.
Extend (10 min): Students use Step through to solve a new case by hand, compare it with the panel, and then explain what Remove support B shows about the moment equation.
assessment: Students calculate the reactions for a 30 ft span with a 9,000 lb load 10 ft from A, and verify the answer by taking moments about B.
Students explain in two sentences why a beam with only one support cannot be in equilibrium under an off-center load.
